exam.title: Analysis I - Beginner Exam
exam.subtitle: Fundamentals of Analysis
exam.instructions: Answer all questions. Show all work and calculations. Permitted aids: Non-programmable calculator. Good luck!

exercises.title: Computing limits
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Factor and cancel
Substituting gives $\frac00$. With $x^2 - 9 = (x-3)(x+3)$ (third binomial formula) we get $\frac{x^2-9}{x-3} = x + 3$ for $x \neq 3$. So the limit is $6$.

Step 2: Part b): Factor out the highest power
$\frac{3n^2 + 2n}{n^2 + 1} = \frac{3 + 2/n}{1 + 1/n^2} \to \frac{3 + 0}{1 + 0} = 3$.

Step 3: Part c): Expand with the conjugate
$\frac{\sqrt{1+x}-1}{x}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{1+x}+1}{\sqrt{1+x}+1} = \frac{(1+x) - 1}{x(\sqrt{1+x}+1)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}+1} \to \frac{1}{2}$.

Step 4: Check with l'Hôpital
a) $\frac{2x}{1}\big|_{x=3} = 6$ ✓. c) $\frac{\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+x}}}{1}\big|_{x=0} = \frac12$ ✓. Remember: for $\frac00$ first simplify algebraically, l'Hôpital as a check.

exercises.title: Rules of differentiation
exercises.description:
Differentiate:
a) $f(x) = x^3\ln x$
b) $g(x) = \sin(3x^2+1)$
c) $h(x) = \dfrac{x^2+1}{x-1}$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Product rule
$u = x^3$, $v = \ln x$: $f'(x) = 3x^2\ln x + x^3\cdot\frac1x = 3x^2\ln x + x^2 = x^2(3\ln x + 1)$.

Step 2: Part b): Chain rule
Outer $\sin u$, inner $3x^2 + 1$: $g'(x) = \cos(3x^2+1)\cdot6x = 6x\cos(3x^2+1)$. (Do not forget the inner derivative $6x$.)

Step 3: Part c): Quotient rule
$h'(x) = \frac{2x(x-1) - (x^2+1)\cdot1}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{x^2 - 2x - 1}{(x-1)^2}$.

Step 4: Numerical check for c)
At $x = 2$: $h(2) = 5$; $h(2.001) = \frac{5.004001}{1.001} \approx 4.99900$; slope $\approx -1.0$; formula: $\frac{4 - 4 - 1}{1} = -1$ ✓.

exercises.title: Continuity and differentiability
exercises.description:
Let $f(x) = \begin{cases}x^2+1 & x < 1\\ 3x-1 & x \geq 1\end{cases}$.
a) Is $f$ continuous at $x_0 = 1$?
b) Is $f$ differentiable at $x_0 = 1$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Continuity condition
$f$ is continuous at $x_0$ if $\lim_{x\to x_0^-}f = \lim_{x\to x_0^+}f = f(x_0)$.

Step 2: Part a): Limits
Left: $\lim_{x\to1^-}(x^2+1) = 2$. Right: $\lim_{x\to1^+}(3x-1) = 2$. Function value: $f(1) = 3 - 1 = 2$. All three values agree: $f$ is **continuous** at $1$.

Step 3: Part b): One-sided derivatives
Left: $f'_-(1) = (x^2+1)'|_{x=1} = 2x|_{x=1} = 2$. Right: $f'_+(1) = (3x-1)'|_{x=1} = 3$.

Step 4: Conclusion
$2 \neq 3$: $f$ is **not differentiable** at $1$ (a kink). The graph has no unique tangent there. Remember: differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous, but not conversely.

exercises.title: Curve sketching of a polynomial
exercises.description:
Examine $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x$:
a) zeros,
b) local extrema,
c) inflection point.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Zeros
$f(x) = x(x^2 - 6x + 9) = x(x-3)^2$. Zeros: $x = 0$ (simple) and $x = 3$ (double, the graph touches the $x$-axis).

Step 2: Part b): Critical points
$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x-1)(x-3)$, so $f'(x) = 0 \iff x \in \{1,3\}$.

Step 3: Part b): Type of extrema
$f''(x) = 6x - 12$. $f''(1) = -6 < 0$: local **maximum** $(1,4)$. $f''(3) = 6 > 0$: local **minimum** $(3,0)$.

Step 4: Part c): Inflection point
$f''(x) = 0 \iff x = 2$ with sign change ($f'' < 0$ left, $> 0$ right). $f(2) = 8 - 24 + 18 = 2$: inflection point $(2,2)$.

Step 5: Plausibility check
The inflection point lies exactly midway between the extrema ($x = 2 = \frac{1+3}{2}$): typical for cubic functions. $f(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 = 4$ ✓.

exercises.title: Computing integrals
exercises.description:
Compute:
a) $\displaystyle\int(2x^3 - 5x + 4)\,dx$
b) $\displaystyle\int_0^1xe^{x^2}\,dx$
c) $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Integrate term by term
$\int(2x^3 - 5x + 4)\,dx = \frac{x^4}{2} - \frac{5x^2}{2} + 4x + C$. Check by differentiating: $2x^3 - 5x + 4$ ✓.

Step 2: Part b): Substitution
$u = x^2$, $du = 2x\,dx$, limits $0 \to 0$, $1 \to 1$: $\int_0^1xe^{x^2}dx = \frac12\int_0^1e^u\,du = \frac12(e - 1)$.

Step 3: Part c): Integration by parts
$u = x$, $v' = \cos x$, so $u' = 1$, $v = \sin x$: $\int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x - \int\sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C$.

Step 4: Checks
b) Numerically: $\frac12(2.71828 - 1) = 0.8591$; the integrand lies between $0$ and $e \approx 2.7$, plausible. c) $(x\sin x + \cos x)' = \sin x + x\cos x - \sin x = x\cos x$ ✓.

exercises.title: Convergence of sequences and series
exercises.description:
a) Show with the $\varepsilon$-definition: $a_n = \frac{2n+1}{n+3} \to 2$.
b) Compute $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n(n+1)}$.
c) Examine $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{n}{2^n}$ with the ratio test.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Estimate the distance
$|a_n - 2| = \left|\frac{2n + 1 - 2n - 6}{n+3}\right| = \frac{5}{n+3} < \varepsilon \iff n > \frac5\varepsilon - 3$. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ (e.g. $N > \frac5\varepsilon$) such that $|a_n - 2| < \varepsilon$ for $n \geq N$.

Step 2: Part b): Telescoping sum
$\frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac1n - \frac1{n+1}$, so $s_N = \sum_{n=1}^N\left(\frac1n - \frac1{n+1}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{N+1} \to 1$.

Step 3: Part c): Ratio test
$\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{(n+1)/2^{n+1}}{n/2^n} = \frac{n+1}{2n} \to \frac12 < 1$. The series converges absolutely.

Step 4: Check
b) $s_3 = \frac12 + \frac16 + \frac1{12} = 0.75 = 1 - \frac14$ ✓. c) The sum is $2$: partial sums $0.5; 1.0; 1.375; 1.625; \dots \to 2$.
